title: Multivariable & Vector Calculus
subject: Calculus
summary: Vectors and coordinates in 3D, partial derivatives and optimisation, multiple integrals with Jacobians, line and surface integrals, and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss. Built around the calculus of electromagnetism and thermodynamics, with explicit chemistry hooks (exact differentials, Maxwell relations, Boltzmann via Lagrange, orbital volume elements).

units.title: Vectors, Coordinates, and Curves in Space
units.summary: Parametric curves, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, vector algebra in 3D (dot and cross products, lines and planes), and vector-valued functions for motion; the geometric language of every physics course after this one.

lessons.title: Parametric curves: slope, concavity, and arc length
objectives: Parametrise a curve (line, circle, ellipse, cycloid, helix projection) and eliminate the parameter when possible.
Compute dy/dx and d^2y/dx^2 for a parametric curve and the arc length integral of sqrt(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2).

lectures.title: Session 17 Clip: General Parametric Equations and the Cycloid
Lec 5: Parametric equations for lines and curves

lessons.title: Polar coordinates: area, arc length, and conic sections
objectives: Convert between polar and Cartesian coordinates, sketch r = f(theta) for standard curves, and compute the area enclosed, (1/2) integral r^2 d theta.
Write the arc length in polar form and the slope of a polar curve.
Identify conic sections in polar form r = ed/(1 + e cos theta) and relate eccentricity to orbit shape.

lessons.title: Vectors in 3D and the dot product: angle, projection, and work
objectives: Perform vector addition, scaling and decomposition into components in 3D, and compute magnitudes and unit vectors.
Compute the dot product, the angle between vectors, and the scalar and vector projections; interpret W = F . d.

lectures.title: Session 3: Uses of the dot product lengths and angles

lessons.title: The cross product, torque, and the scalar triple product
objectives: Compute the cross product by determinant and by the right-hand rule, and interpret |a x b| as parallelogram area and the torque tau = r x F.
Evaluate the scalar triple product a . (b x c) as a volume and as a determinant, and state when three vectors are coplanar.
keyEquations: \vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\det[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]
demoIdeas: Drag two vectors in 3D to see the cross-product arrow and parallelogram area; add a third vector to show the parallelepiped volume and the coplanar case when it vanishes.

lessons.title: Index notation: the Kronecker delta, Levi-Civita symbol, and vector identities
objectives: Use the Kronecker delta and Levi-Civita symbol to write (a x b)_i = eps_ijk a_j b_k and verify a . (b x c) = b . (c x a).
Derive the BAC-CAB rule a x (b x c) = b(a . c) - c(a . b) from the contraction identity eps_ijk eps_ilm = delta_jl delta_km - delta_jm delta_kl.
keyEquations: \vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)

lessons.title: Lines, planes, and quadric surfaces in 3D
objectives: Write parametric, vector and symmetric equations of a line in 3D and the equation of a plane from a point and a normal vector.
Find the angle between planes, the distance from a point to a plane, and the intersection of a line and a plane.
Identify and sketch quadric surfaces (ellipsoid, hyperboloid, paraboloid, cone, cylinder) from their equations using traces.

lessons.title: Cylindrical and spherical coordinates
objectives: Convert between Cartesian, cylindrical (r, theta, z), and spherical (rho, theta, phi) coordinates, stating the physics convention for theta and phi.
Describe a region such as a sphere, cone, or cylinder in the most convenient coordinate system, e.g. an atomic orbital's volume element.
demoIdeas: Coordinate-system switcher: drag a point in 3D and see (x, y, z), (r, phi, z), and (rho, theta, phi) with the coordinate surfaces highlighted.

lessons.title: Vector-valued functions: velocity, speed, arc length, and the helix
objectives: Differentiate and integrate vector-valued functions r(t) component-wise and state the product rules for dot and cross products.
Compute the tangent vector T, speed, and arc length of a space curve, and parametrise by arc length.
Describe the helix as a model for a charged particle in a magnetic field with r(t) = (R cos wt, R sin wt, vz t).

lessons.title: Curvature, acceleration components, and central-force motion
objectives: Compute curvature kappa = |dT/ds| and decompose acceleration into tangential and normal components.
Derive the constancy of the angular momentum direction for a central force from r x p and show that r x r-dot = const implies motion in a plane (Kepler's second law).

units.title: Partial Derivatives and Optimisation
units.summary: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, the total differential and chain rule, the gradient and directional derivative, and constrained optimisation with Lagrange multipliers; the calculus of thermodynamics (exact differentials, Maxwell relations) and of the Boltzmann distribution.

lessons.title: Functions of several variables: level sets, limits, and continuity
objectives: Describe a function of two or three variables with level curves, level surfaces and cross-sections, e.g. isotherms of P(V, T) or a potential-energy surface.
Define limits and continuity in several variables and show a limit fails to exist by comparing two paths.

lectures.title: Session 24: Functions of two variables graphs
Session 25: Level curves and contour plots

lessons.title: Partial derivatives, mixed partials, and what is held fixed
objectives: Compute partial derivatives, including higher-order and mixed partials, and state Clairaut's theorem that the mixed partials are equal for smooth functions.
Interpret a partial derivative with its held-fixed variables made explicit, e.g. (dU/dT) at constant V versus at constant P.
Check whether a function satisfies a PDE such as Laplace's equation by computing second partials.

lessons.title: Tangent planes, linear approximation, and the total differential
objectives: Find the equation of the tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at a point and use it as a linear approximation.
Write the total differential df = f_x dx + f_y dy and use it to propagate errors in a function of several measured variables.
demoIdeas: Surface with a tangent plane at a draggable point and the linear-estimate error against step size; sliders for the uncertainty in r and h propagate to V = pi r^2 h.

lessons.title: The chain rule, implicit differentiation, reciprocity, and the Leibniz rule
objectives: Apply the chain rule to compositions with several intermediate variables, drawing a dependency tree.
Differentiate implicitly using F(x, y, z) = 0, dz/dx = -F_x/F_z, and verify the triple-product (reciprocity) relation (dx/dy)_z (dy/dz)_x (dz/dx)_y = -1 on the ideal gas law.
State and apply the Leibniz rule for differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter.
keyEquations: \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)_z\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\right)_x\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)_y=-1

lessons.title: The gradient, directional derivatives, and steepest ascent
objectives: Compute the gradient of a scalar field in Cartesian coordinates and state that it is perpendicular to level sets.
Compute the directional derivative D_u f = grad f . u and find the direction of steepest ascent and its rate.
Relate the gradient to the total differential, df = grad f . dr.

lessons.title: Tangent planes to level surfaces and force from potential energy

Compute the force F = -grad V from a potential energy and verify with a 2D example such as a harmonic or Coulomb potential.

lessons.title: Critical points, the Hessian test, closed regions, and least squares
objectives: Find critical points of f(x, y) and classify them with the second-derivative (Hessian) test, including saddles.
Find global extrema on a closed region by checking the interior and the boundary.
Fit a line by least squares by minimising the sum of squared residuals as a function of the two parameters.

lessons.title: Lagrange multipliers and the Boltzmann distribution

units.title: Multiple Integrals
units.summary: Double and triple integrals in Cartesian, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, centres of mass and moments of inertia (rotational spectroscopy), and change of variables with Jacobians (volume elements for orbitals and phase space).

objectives: Define the double integral as a limit of Riemann sums and compute it as an iterated integral over rectangles (Fubini's theorem).
Set up and evaluate a double integral over a type I or type II region and exchange the order of integration.
Compute areas, volumes under surfaces, and averages of functions over regions.

units.title: Vector Fields and Line Integrals
units.summary: Vector fields, line integrals and work, conservative fields and potentials (path independence and exact differentials in thermodynamics), and Green's theorem.
